1.pericope_label: The law of the trespass offering

schools.summary: Gill reads the section as supplying the place, the parts and their disposal, the persons liable having been described in the two preceding chapters, and notes that the fat was claimed by God as in the peace and sin offerings.

Henry has the same scarlet-line tradition by way of bishop Patrick, and draws the consequence of the sin offering's rules applying here: the offerer got no share at all, and where a peace offering suited feasting, a trespass offering brought in sorrow for sin suited fasting.
Clarke places the killing on the north side of the altar and refers the rump and the rest back to the earlier chapter, the principal subjects being nearly the same in both.

Ellicott would render the opening simply 'and this is the law', takes the section as giving the priest fuller instructions than the earlier law did, has the offerers themselves slaughter the victim, prefers 'throw' to 'sprinkle' for the blood, and reports the scarlet thread of the second Temple; Keil and Delitzsch make the parallel with the sin offering exact, one law for both since every trespass is a sin, and note that the verses on the burnt and meat offerings are an appendix belonging to the previous chapter.

themes: one law for sin and trespass
the north side of the altar

5.pericope_label: The burning, and the priest's own portion

schools.summary: Gill restricts the flesh to the priests and their sons, not their wives and daughters; Calvin sees the passage confirming the priests' rights and adding a rule against rivalry among them, reserving certain portions to the priest who actually made the atonement — a reward for diligence he calls fatherly indulgence rather than the higher motive, and he cites the prophet's charge that they would not kindle fire for nothing.
Wesley limits the one law to the matter immediately following, the two offerings differing in other things, and identifies the priest's share as the part God allowed him.

Ellicott passes over the burning as already described and draws the working consequence of one law for both offerings: what is omitted from the regulations of the one must be supplied from the directions given for the other.

outliers.claim: the reserved portions were a concession to human weakness — many were drawn to the work by gain who would otherwise have neglected it, and God consulted their infirmity

themes: the priests and no one else
hire as a spur to diligence

8.pericope_label: The skin of the burnt offering, and the meat offerings

schools.summary: Gill gives the plain reason for the grant: in the burnt offering the flesh was wholly consumed, so nothing was left to requite the priest for his trouble.

Clarke traces the right to the skin back through bishop Patrick to Adam's sacrifice and God's clothing of him, then to the Gentile custom of giving skins to priests and the superstitious use of sleeping on them for dreams, citing Virgil and the Highland togharm at length; Wesley supplies the reason for the two rules, that the dressed offering went to the priest who laboured about it while the raw was easier to keep and share out.

Ellicott explains the skin as the only part the fire left, reports the second-Temple rule dividing the skins among the serving course each Sabbath evening, would read the clause about raw flour as 'or dry', and draws from the Hebrew phrase 'a man as his brother' the later rule excluding children and women of priestly descent while admitting a blemished priest.

themes: the only part the fire left

11.pericope_label: The law of the peace offerings

schools.summary: Gill treats the heading as announcing what is still outstanding; Calvin names the whole class the sacrifices of prosperities, since in every case — thanks for a blessing, deliverance sought, piety professed, a vow paid — the offerer was owning God as the author of all good, and marks off the thanksgiving offering as the one kind not always brought.

Henry gives each of the three classes its occasion and observes that none of them was commanded: in the expression of their sense of mercy God left them freer than in the expression of their sense of sin, to try the generosity of their devotion, while the required sacrifices of atonement showed the necessity of the great propitiation.

Ellicott sets the section in the pattern he has traced twice already, fuller priestly directions following the people's instructions, and flags the subjectless Hebrew verb as better carried in English by an impersonal or a passive.

12.pericope_label: The thanksgiving offering and its four kinds of bread

schools.summary: Gill reports Jarchi and Aben Ezra confining the thanksgiving to deliverance out of distress and declines to narrow it that far, allowing it for the common mercies of life; on the heave offering he takes one from each sort, with Aben Ezra and Maimonides.

Wesley confines the ban on leaven to what went on the altar and finds the reason for this bread in the occasion itself; Clarke offers two accounts of the same-day rule, the heat of the country and Harmer's suggestion that the law was aimed at the drying of devoted flesh.

Ellicott reads the silence about quantities as leaving them to those who administered the law, reports the second-Temple reckoning of forty cakes with four to the priest, notes Pentecost as the only other leavened offering, and takes the eating-limit as encouraging liberality to the poor while keeping the meal a sacred feast; Keil and Delitzsch supply the memorial portion the text leaves unmentioned and name the priest who took the heave offering.

debates.question: How far does the occasion for a thanksgiving offering extend?

sides.position: to notable deliverances only — from the sea, from travel, from prison, from violent disease
to the common mercies of life, or any particular instance of goodness a man was sensible of

16.pericope_label: The vow and the freewill offering

schools.summary: Gill takes the third-day remainder as what was left uneaten on the second; Calvin argues that the vow meant here is a simple and not a conditional one, since a conditional vow paid would be thanksgiving and fall under the first head, and gives two reasons for the time limit — that the meats should not turn and bring religion into contempt, and that a man free to salt and keep them might make an ostentatious offering at no real cost.
Wesley marks the extra day as the permission the thank offering did not have, and reads the clause about imputing as meaning the offering will not stand as acceptable service.

Ellicott draws the canon-law distinction between a vow that binds the man until he fulfils it and a freewill offering that binds only the animal devoted, explains the extra day by these offerings being supplication for favours still to come, makes the owner responsible for the rule being kept, and reads 'abomination' from the climate; Keil and Delitzsch note that the word is used of sacrificial flesh alone and properly means a stench.

debates.question: What distinguishes this second class of peace offering?

sides.position: the vow binds the person until fulfilled, the freewill offering only the animal devoted
the vow meant here is a simple one, since a conditional vow paid is thanksgiving and belongs to the first class

themes: a second day, not a third

schools.summary: Gill lists the defilements that might reach the flesh in transit and those that disqualified a man — a dead body, a bone of one, the grave it lay in; Calvin meets the charge of severity directly, refusing the softening of 'cut off' into expulsion from the camp, since a man who sinned in error escaped the sentence and it fell only on open contempt of holy things.

Clarke glosses having one's uncleanness upon him as not having washed and bathed since the defilement, and adds the cutaneous disorders the law covers; Wesley limits the general word to the holy offering, separates the two verses by whether the uncleanness arose within a man or without, and confines the penalty to eating knowingly.

Ellicott would render the permission as every clean person may eat, so that anyone the offerer invited might share; Keil and Delitzsch enumerate the sources of defilement and take 'abomination' to include the unclean fishes, birds and smaller creatures.

themes: why the sentence is not excessive

schools.summary: Gill takes the blood prohibition to cover clean creatures as much as unclean and reports the Jewish reading of it as aimed at the limb torn from a living beast; Calvin looks past the boundary to the purpose, that forbidding fat at ordinary meals kept piety alive at the daily table far from the temple, and declines the allegories other interpreters indulge in here.

Wesley confines the general rule to the sacrificial kinds and heads off the objection that the clause about fallen beasts is superfluous; Clarke gives the reason for the three kinds, notes that fat in general was among the blessings God gave the people, and reads being cut off as excommunication from their inheritance.

Ellicott extends the fat ban to the three kinds even when killed for private eating, reports the three fats the second Temple held a man liable for and the finer distinctions built on them, binds the blood law on Israelites wherever they dwell, and notes that excision was inflicted only for the life-blood; Keil and Delitzsch allow the fat of fallen or torn cattle to any common use though never to be eaten.

28.pericope_label: The wave breast and the heave shoulder

schools.summary: Gill itemises the fat that went to the fire and identifies the priest with the claim on the shoulder as the one who had sprinkled the blood and burnt the fat.

Henry reads the lifting up and the waving as two distinct confessions, of God as the God of heaven and as Lord of the whole earth, and takes the breast and shoulder for the affections and the actions which God's people owe to his honour and his priests to the church.

Wesley describes the priest putting the parts into the offerer's hands and supporting them through the waving, explains why offerings only partly burnt are still called offerings made by fire, extends the grant to every succeeding high priest, and takes the breast for wisdom and the shoulder for strength in action.

Ellicott sets out the whole rite as performed in the time of Christ, down to the order in which the parts were stacked on the owner's hands and the rules for partners and for women; Keil and Delitzsch read the two portions as a tribute imposed on Israel and given to the priests as a right claimable for all ages.

themes: heaven and earth in two motions

schools.summary: Gill takes the anointing to stand for the office and reports Aben Ezra's stronger reading, that the portion is the reward of faithful performance, and lists what it came to.

Henry reads the grant's timing as the point — provision made on the very day of ordination — and generalises it: God will see that those employed for him are well provided for, since his work is its own wages and there is a present reward of obedience in obedience; and he turns the second verse into a statute binding the people to give the priests their share cheerfully.
Wesley doubles the figure, the anointing put for the priesthood and then for the share belonging to the priest by virtue of it; Clarke refers the day of the anointing back to the consecration itself.

Ellicott cuts through the figure and would render it simply the share of Aaron and the share of his sons, and makes the command binding on every offerer since the portion is the priests' by right of office; Keil and Delitzsch treat the two verses as the hinge into the closing summary.

themes: provision on the day of ordination

37.pericope_label: The summary of the sacrificial law

schools.summary: Gill argues that 'in mount Sinai' should be by or near the mount, since these laws were given after the tabernacle was erected and out of it, and enters the further qualification that the verse speaks of the command to sacrifice given in the wilderness, not of sacrifices actually offered there; Calvin finds the point of the summary in what it forecloses, full provision having been made against any human invention insinuating itself, from which he infers how earnestly all temerity in invention is to be avoided.

Wesley takes the consecrations for the sacrifice offered at the consecration of the priests; Clarke holds that the laws were probably given while Moses was on the mount, the eighty days being ample, and uses the summary as the occasion for a glossary in which the derivations carry his reading of each rite.

Ellicott indexes every offering to its own chapter and supplement and would render the consecrations as the offering of consecration, the high priest's meat offering on entering office; Keil and Delitzsch note that the fill-offering appears here though instituted earlier, and explain its name from the phrase about filling the hand.

sides.position: by or near the mount, out of the tabernacle after it was erected
probably on the mount itself, during the eighty days Moses spent there

debates.question: What is "the law of the consecrations"?

sides.position: the high priest's meat offering on entering the pontifical office
the sacrifice offered at the consecration of the priests

themes: on the mount or by it
